title: Retrieval lab: choose the control from the symptom
goal: Retrieve the first certification cycle without hints and separate delivered coverage from evidence still missing.
tag: Certification retrieval + gap session · cycle 1 of 7
concept:
This is the fire-drill day. You are given a symptom, not a feature name. Your job is to choose the next control and explain what evidence would prove it worked.

The six prior lessons covered recovery, access paths, pruning, nested data, orchestration gates, and one combined repair. Retrieval matters because an exam or incident will not label the chapter for you.
example: Orders batch B23 has four symptoms: a retry repeated output, an analyst cannot read the candidate, a date filter scans almost everything, and publish ran after validation failed. The correct response is not “optimize the pipeline.” Each symptom points to a different mechanism and a different proof.

use_case.when: Use a retrieval-and-gap session after a run of focused lessons to test whether you can select controls from symptoms without feature-name prompts.
use_case.example: Triage a failed orders pipeline by matching duplicate output, denied access, poor pruning, and unsafe publish to different remedies.
use_case.decision: Count an area as delivered when the lesson exists. Count it as retained only after a fresh private answer or real sandbox action; silence is not evidence of mastery or failure.

practice: Choose one B23 symptom. Predict the control, reveal it, and name the missing vendor evidence before moving on.
boundary: The browser is an open-book local JavaScript retrieval coach. It cannot measure memory, exam readiness, product UI skill, permissions, performance, or the result of vendor execution.

Symptom
'+incidentSymptom.options?.[incidentSymptom.selectedIndex]?.textContent+'
Control
'+(revealed?c[0]:'Predict before reveal')+'
Required evidence
'+(revealed?c[2]:'Not revealed')+'
';}incidentSymptom.onchange=()=>{revealed=false;retrievalPaint()};revealControl.onclick=()=>{revealed=true;retrievalPaint()};retrievalPaint();
questions: A date predicate scans every data chunk. First move?
Increase compute
Inspect pruning evidence and recorded ranges
Add a publish task
Measure whether layout metadata can exclude data before changing compute or clustering.
Validation failed but publish ran. Which boundary failed?
Orchestration dependency
JSON parsing
Table ownership only
The workflow allowed an unsafe transition.
What can this public retrieval page establish about personal mastery?
Complete readiness
Nothing without explicit fresh private evidence
A failed exam
Delivered curriculum and personal mastery remain separate.

steps.note: Map four incident signals to distinct control families.
Name the proof required for each control.
Retrieve one decision from the symptom, not from a feature name.

walkthrough.limit: Executed local Python over a synthetic retrieval map. It did not grade a learner or run either vendor platform.

sources: Databricks Data Engineer Associate exam guide
visual_explanation: The three columns force the decision sequence: observe the symptom, choose one control family, then demand proof. Changing the symptom replaces all three rather than decorating a fixed template.

Which vendor action still needs real sandbox evidence this week?

product_sections.title: Databricks retrieval: identify the next evidence-producing action
product_sections.html:
Use case. A Lakeflow job is green at ingest, but the gold result is wrong. Select the next evidence-producing action rather than naming random features.

Prepared real lab. Use an authorized non-production workspace, job identity, Unity Catalog objects, and a small synthetic batch. Compute can incur cost.

The SQL/YAML is unexecuted vendor practice.

SELECT try_parse_json(payload) AS v FROM bronze.b23;SELECT event_id, count(*) FROM bronze.b23 GROUP BY event_id HAVING count(*)>1;-- inspect job task: publish depends_on validate; run_if: ALL_SUCCESS-- then compare candidate counts before promotion

Failure/fix. A green ingest task is weak evidence. Query the failing invariant, preserve the source/checkpoint, repair in isolation, and test that the publish dependency blocks failure. This does not assess workspace navigation or hands-on speed.
product_sections.markdown:
Authorized Databricks sandbox; SQL/YAML unexecuted.

```sql
SELECT try_parse_json(payload) AS v FROM bronze.b23;
SELECT event_id, count(*) FROM bronze.b23 GROUP BY event_id HAVING count(*) > 1;
-- publish depends on validate with ALL_SUCCESS
```

Choose the query/control from the symptom, then run it in a real sandbox separately.

product_sections.title: Snowflake retrieval: choose the query, privilege, or task evidence
product_sections.html:
Use case. The same B23 outcome can come from bad parsing, a missing privilege path, poor pruning, or an unsafe task graph. Retrieve the smallest diagnostic that separates them.

Prepared real lab. Use an authorized non-production database/schema, role, warehouse, and task graph. Warehouse and task execution can incur credits.

The SQL is unexecuted vendor practice.

SELECT TRY_PARSE_JSON(payload) v FROM bronze.b23;SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE b23_pipeline;SELECT * FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.QUERY_HISTORY()) ORDER BY start_time DESC;SELECT * FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COMPLETE_TASK_GRAPHS()) ORDER BY scheduled_time DESC;

Failure/fix. Granting broad ownership or increasing warehouse size can hide the symptom without proving the cause. Inspect the narrow path, then test both the intended success and denial/failure case.

';$('sfState').textContent=show?'Local retrieval reveal; no Snowflake SQL ran.':'Choose before revealing.';}sfGap.onchange=()=>sfPaint(false);sfNext.onclick=()=>sfPaint(true);sfPaint(false);

title: Silence raises suspicion; it does not prove a node is dead
goal: Turn heartbeat delay into an adjustable suspicion score instead of one brittle timeout.
concept:
A friend who usually replies in one minute is concerning after five minutes. A friend who often replies in ten minutes is not. The same silence means different things because history differs.

A phi-accrual detector converts time since the last heartbeat into a suspicion score. The application chooses a threshold. A lower threshold reacts faster but causes more false suspicions.
example: Node B normally replies around every 1 second. At 1.2 seconds, suspicion is modest. At 4 seconds, it is high. Under a noisy network with wider historical variation, the same 1.2-second pause should look less alarming.

use_case.when: Use adaptive suspicion when cluster heartbeat timing varies and downstream policies need a continuous confidence signal.
use_case.example: An Akka cluster monitors JVM nodes across a network where occasional pauses are normal.
use_case.decision: Use phi to separate measurement from policy. Do not equate “unreachable” with “permanently failed”; membership removal still needs a coordinated policy.

practice: Change elapsed silence and network variability. Predict whether phi crosses the policy threshold.
boundary: This browser uses the documented normal-distribution formula with a fixed mean and standard deviation. Real detectors learn a sample window and add acceptable pause/minimum-deviation controls.
js:
function erf(x){const s=Math.sign(x),a=Math.abs(x),t=1/(1+.3275911*a);return s*(1-(((((1.061405429*t-1.453152027)*t)+1.421413741)*t-0.284496736)*t+.254829592)*Math.exp(-a*a));}function phiPaint(){const elapsed=Number(silence.value)/10,sd=Number(jitter.value)/100,z=(elapsed-1)/(sd*Math.sqrt(2)),cdf=.5*(1+erf(z)),phi=-Math.log10(Math.max(1e-9,1-cdf)),threshold=3;silenceOut.textContent=elapsed.toFixed(1);world.innerHTML='
phi '+phi.toFixed(2)+'

Threshold 3: '+(phi>=threshold?'SUSPECT':'AVAILABLE')+'. Same silence is judged against observed variability.

';}silence.oninput=phiPaint;jitter.onchange=phiPaint;phiPaint();
questions: Lowering the phi threshold does what?
Slower detection and fewer false suspicions
Faster detection and more false suspicions
Creates consensus
The policy fires on less evidence.
Why can noisy history lower suspicion for the same delay?
The delay is less statistically surprising
The clock stops
Heartbeats become durable
Phi is calibrated to the observed arrival distribution.
What does phi not decide?
Suspicion level
Permanent membership removal policy
Heartbeat timing
Measurement and cluster action are different layers.

steps.note: Set learned timing parameters and current silence.
Approximate the normal CDF for this small teaching trace.
Convert tail probability into suspicion and apply policy.

walkthrough.limit: Executed on local Java 17 using synthetic timing parameters and a logistic CDF approximation. It did not instantiate Akka or learn heartbeat samples.

sources: JAIST: The phi accrual failure detector
visual_explanation: The suspicion meter changes with both elapsed silence and historical jitter, making the central idea visible: the same delay is not equally surprising in every network.
written_questions: Which pause in your runtime would create legitimate heartbeat delay?
Who should own the policy that turns suspicion into traffic removal?

title: Let the new system observe production before production observes it
goal: Use shadow traffic to compare a migration target without letting its responses affect customers.
concept:
A trainee can prepare every restaurant order beside the chef while only the chef’s plate reaches the customer. You learn from real demand without exposing the trainee’s mistakes.

Shadowing copies requests to the new path. The old path still owns the response. Compare outputs, latency, errors, and side effects before moving real traffic.
example: The legacy pricing API returns $25 for request r-23. The new API returns $27. Customers still receive $25. The mismatch becomes evidence to investigate, not an accidental rollout.

use_case.when: Use shadowing when a replacement can process representative production inputs safely and you need evidence beyond synthetic tests.
use_case.example: Run a new lineage parser beside the existing parser and compare emitted edges without publishing the candidate graph.
use_case.decision: Shadow read-only or isolated behavior first. If the candidate can trigger payments, emails, writes, or quotas, stub or redirect those effects before copying traffic.

practice: Toggle whether candidate side effects are isolated, then compare a matching and mismatching response.
boundary: Shadowing does not test customer-visible behavior, writes, long-term state, authorization differences, or full load unless explicitly designed. Duplicating traffic can add cost and privacy risk.
js:
function shadowPaint(){const match=shadowOutput.value==='25',safe=effects.value==='isolated';world.innerHTML='

'+(!safe?'Unsafe shadow: copied request can duplicate effects.':match?'Comparable output matched.':'Safe mismatch evidence; customer still received legacy result.')+'

';}shadowOutput.onchange=shadowPaint;effects.onchange=shadowPaint;shadowPaint();
questions: Shadow returns $27; legacy returns $25. What sees the customer?
Both
The legacy path still owns the response.
What must be isolated before shadowing a create call?
Side effects
Metrics
Request IDs
Copied writes can duplicate real-world actions.
What does a perfect shadow comparison not prove?
Candidate handled observed inputs
Customer-visible cutover and stateful writes are safe
Outputs matched
Shadowing deliberately omits some production effects.

steps.note: Record one request and both outputs.

steps.code:
customer_response=legacy
diff={k:(legacy.get(k),shadow.get(k)) for k in legacy if legacy.get(k)!=shadow.get(k)}
steps.note: Keep legacy authoritative while computing differences.
Turn disagreement into migration evidence, not customer exposure.

walkthrough.limit: Executed local Python over synthetic responses. It did not mirror network traffic or isolate real side effects.

visual_explanation: The request forks, but only the upper legacy arrow reaches the customer. The lower box turns red when effects are live, revealing the central migration boundary.
written_questions: Which side effect makes one of your services unsafe to shadow today?
What mismatch rate and categories would justify a cutover decision?

title: Return “input required,” then retry the same tool call
goal: Understand MCP multi-round-trip requests without hidden transport session state.
concept:
A clerk pauses an application and hands back a numbered form for the missing signature. You return the signed form with the same case number.

In MCP 2026-07-28, a server can return input_required with requests and opaque requestState. The client fulfills them and retries the original method with inputResponses.
example: book_table(date=Friday) lacks party size. The server returns an elicitation plus state s23. The client asks the user, receives 4, and retries the same tool call with that answer and state. The server then returns the final booking.

use_case.when: Use MRTR when a tool, prompt, or resource needs user input, sampling, or roots during one logical operation over a stateless protocol.
use_case.example: A booking tool requests party size only after checking that Friday has availability.
use_case.decision: Use explicit input-required rounds for protocol-visible interaction. Use a separate durable task when work is long-running, and never auto-answer sensitive elicitation without user-facing policy.

practice: Step through initial call, input-required result, user response, and retry. Watch what the server must carry explicitly.
boundary: The model omits protocol negotiation, cancellation, max-round limits, authentication, sensitive-field UI, errors, and SDK-specific callback behavior.
js:
let mrtrStep=0;const msgs=[['Client → server','tools/call book_table(Friday)'],['Server → client','input_required · party_size? · state=s23'],['Client → user','How many people? → 4'],['Client → server','retry same call · inputResponses=4 · state=s23'],['Server → client','final booking b-900']];function mrtrPaint(){world.innerHTML='

'+msgs[mrtrStep][0]+': '+msgs[mrtrStep][1]+'

';mrtrNext.disabled=mrtrStep===4;}mrtrNext.onclick=()=>{mrtrStep=Math.min(4,mrtrStep+1);mrtrPaint()};mrtrReset.onclick=()=>{mrtrStep=0;mrtrPaint()};mrtrPaint();
questions: What does the client retry after fulfilling input?
A new unrelated method
The original request with inputResponses and requestState
Only a websocket
MRTR continues one logical operation by retrying the original request.
Why echo opaque requestState?
To expose secrets to the model
To carry server continuation state explicitly
To replace authentication
The stateless transport does not hide continuation state.
When is MRTR the wrong mechanism?
One missing user parameter
A long-running durable job needing independent lifecycle
One sampling request
Durable asynchronous work belongs in a task lifecycle.

steps.note: Create the initial tool call.
Server returns explicit continuation state and a requested input.
Client retries the original call with the answer and state.
Server produces the final result.

walkthrough.limit: Executed local Python over synthetic protocol dictionaries. It did not use an MCP SDK or contact a server.

visual_explanation: The sequence diagram shows the original call returning rather than holding a stream. State and answers visibly travel back on the retry.
written_questions: Which of your tools currently hides continuation state in a session?
What elicitation must always stop for explicit user review?

title: Scan the room, train in its twin, then try the real pickup
goal: Understand the evidence and transfer boundary in Splat2Act scene-personalized robot manipulation.
concept:
A driving student can practice in a model of the exact neighborhood before touching the real car. Splat2Act applies that idea to robot manipulation.

A phone scan builds a photorealistic scene and collision geometry. A simulation oracle generates successful demonstrations. A VLA policy is adapted in two stages, then deployed back into the captured environment.
example: The paper reports 0% pickup success for an unadapted generalist policy in captured deployment scenes. Its strongest personalized policy reached 62.5% aggregate pickup success. On a 12-task subset, reported real-robot success was 63.9% versus 66.7% in simulation.

use_case.when: Potentially useful when a robot must adapt to a specific building and object set, while collecting many real demonstrations is expensive.
use_case.example: Personalize a mobile manipulator for shelves and counters in one office using phone scans and object images.
use_case.decision: Treat this as recent research. Require safety review, new-scene replication, failure analysis, and real-world evaluation before operational use.

practice: Move through capture, synthetic demonstrations, personalization, and real deployment. Notice which stages generate evidence versus assumptions.
boundary: The browser replays reported aggregate metrics and pipeline stages. It does not reconstruct a scene, simulate physics, train a VLA, measure safety, or reproduce the paper.

'+stages.map((s,i)=>'
'+s[0]+'
'+s[1]+'
').join('')+'

'+(n===4?'Transfer boundary: simulation success is evidence, not a guarantee of safe real behavior.':'Current artifact: '+stages[n][1])+'

';}robotStage.oninput=robotPaint;robotPaint();

To inspect transfer, not assume it

title: Rollback is another deployment—of the last known-good digest
goal: Restore a known artifact through the same protected path instead of rebuilding or bypassing controls.
concept:
A restaurant recalls today’s sauce and reopens yesterday’s sealed batch. It does not try to recreate yesterday’s sauce from memory during the incident.

A rollback selects the last known-good immutable digest and deploys it through the production environment gate. It records a new deployment event. It does not erase history.
example: Production runs sha256:bad23. Error rate crosses the rollback threshold. The workflow selects recorded digest sha256:good22, requires production approval, deploys it, and verifies recovery. Rebuilding commit 22 could create different bytes.

use_case.when: Use artifact rollback when the previous version remains compatible with current data, schema, and external contracts.
use_case.example: Restore the prior API container after a new image raises 5xx errors.
use_case.decision: Rollback code only when backward compatibility holds. Use roll-forward or explicit data repair when migrations or irreversible side effects make the old artifact unsafe.

practice: Toggle schema compatibility and choose rollback or roll-forward. Watch whether the previous digest is actually safe.
boundary: The browser models artifact selection and compatibility as two values. Production rollback needs health criteria, deployment history, approvals, credentials, traffic strategy, data checks, and post-restore verification.
js:
function rollbackPaint(){const safe=schemaCompat.value==='yes';world.innerHTML='

'+(safe?'Rollback is a new protected deployment of good22.':'Choose roll-forward or data-compatible recovery; digest identity alone is insufficient.')+'

';}schemaCompat.onchange=rollbackPaint;rollbackPaint();

It can produce different bytes
Git forbids it
Approvals disappear
The verified object is the immutable prior artifact.
Destructive schema migration broke old-code compatibility. Best default?
Deploy old code anyway
Roll forward or repair compatibility first
Delete history
Artifact rollback cannot undo incompatible state.
What should GitHub environment history show?
Only the original deployment
A new rollback deployment and its result
No record
Rollback is an auditable production action.

steps.note: Record immutable deployment history and state compatibility.

steps.code: candidate=next(x for x in reversed(history) if x["healthy"])
steps.note: Select the last known-good artifact.
Choose rollback only when the old artifact can run against current state.

visual_explanation: The curved arrow points from the failing deployment to the exact prior digest; compatibility changes whether that arrow is green or blocked.

title: Deprecated is a warning; Sunset is the shutdown date
goal: Signal API lifecycle separately: when use became discouraged and when service is expected to stop.
concept:
A train station can announce “this route is being retired” before it posts “last train: December 1.” Those are different facts.

The HTTP Deprecation response header signals that a resource is or will be deprecated. Sunset communicates when it is expected to become unresponsive. A Link can point to migration guidance.
example: GET /v1/orders returns Deprecation: @1790812800, Sunset: Tue, 01 Dec 2026 00:00:00 GMT, and a link to the v2 guide. Clients can warn owners before the deadline instead of discovering removal through a 404.

use_case.when: Use lifecycle headers when an API version or resource has active consumers that need machine-readable migration notice.
use_case.example: A gateway inventories callers still using /v1/orders and alerts teams before the announced sunset.
use_case.decision: Headers complement—not replace—direct owner communication, telemetry, compatibility testing, and a rollback plan. Do not announce a date you cannot support operationally.

practice: Move the current date before deprecation, between deprecation and sunset, and after sunset. Observe the client action.
boundary: The browser uses fixed dates. RFC 9745 does not force a server to stop at sunset, guarantee client support, or define organization-specific enforcement and communication.
js:
function lifecyclePaint(){const v=lifecycleDay.value,state=v==='before'?['SUPPORTED','No lifecycle action yet','good']:v==='deprecated'?['DEPRECATED','Warn owner; migrate before Dec 1','warn']:['PAST SUNSET','Do not assume availability; use v2','bad'];world.innerHTML='

'+state[1]+'

';}lifecycleDay.onchange=lifecyclePaint;lifecyclePaint();

The resource is discouraged now or from a stated time
The exact shutdown is guaranteed
Authentication
Deprecation and shutdown time are separate signals.
Which header communicates expected unresponsiveness?
ETag
Sunset
Retry-After
Sunset carries the lifecycle end date.
Why keep direct consumer outreach?
Headers guarantee every client reacts
Many clients do not inspect lifecycle headers
RFCs forbid links
Machine-readable notice is one layer of migration management.

steps.note: Define the two independent lifecycle times.
Place the client between them.

steps.code: state="PAST_SUNSET" if now>=sunset else "DEPRECATED" if now>=deprecation else "SUPPORTED"
steps.note: Derive the action window.
